title: spike-sampler-runbook-and-next-steps-mar20-2026
content:
Summary:

During the 2026-03-19 evening synthetic mixed-workload sweep we observed recurring 95th+ latency spikes (~700–900ms token tail) on warm hosts running the small-batched interactive profile. This doc captures the ad-hoc runbook we used to triage, the lightweight reproduction steps, measured artifacts, hypotheses, short experiments we ran, and the next actions. The goal is a reproducible triage pattern the on-call/bench teams can run without needing deep kernel/infra access.

Observed symptoms (high level):
- Spike pattern: intermittent ~2–8% of tokens per 10k requests show latency 4–6x the baseline.
- Environment: on Dedicated pool n2-small-gpu-1, models: redwood-7b-v2-quant, batching policy: adaptive (max_batch=16, delay_ms=12).
- Time window: first seen 2026-03-19 18:14 UTC, recurring every ~20–45 minutes for ~3 hrs.
- Affected flows: multi-turn chat with prefix caching enabled; single-turn embed requests unaffected.

Quick reproduction (commands we ran):
1) baseline sampler (single process):
   ./tools/sampler --profile mixed_interactive --qps 120 --max_seq 512 --duration 30m --model redwood-7b-v2-quant \
     --batching max_batch=16,delay_ms=12 --warmup 300

2) isolated tail sampler (high variance):
   ./tools/sampler --profile prefix-heavy --qps 80 --concurrency 64 --duration 20m --model redwood-7b-v2-quant --kv-cache on

3) playback from production traces (sanitized):
   python tools/playback.py --trace traces/2026-03-19-prefix-sparse.json --target-host host-0.redwood-dedicated:443 --parallel 16

Key artifacts collected:
- Sampled traces: traces/2026-03-19-prefix-sparse.json (attached to JIRA-PI-3742).
- Perf counters: per-host p95/p99 over time, cpu steal %, nvml GPU utilization timeline, kernel scheduling counts (sched_switch).
- Heap/kv-cache metrics: eviction_rate spiked during the windows by ~1.4x.
- Lightweight flamegraphs from a 90s tracer capture during a spike (flame_spike_1814.svg).

Notable measurements (representative):
- Baseline token latency (median): ~85ms
- Tail during spike (95th): 720ms; 99th: 1.1s
- Batch sizes at spike times: mean_batch=3.8 (down from 6.2 baseline), indicating front-of-queue fragmentation
- CPU run-queue length increased to 7–12 on host-0 for short bursts (10–40ms windows)

What we tried quickly (experiments & results):
1) Disable prefix/KV cache in sampler:
   - Result: spikes frequency dropped by ~60% (indicates cache interaction but not sole cause).
2) Increase batching delay to 30ms for a short run:
   - Result: mean latency increased slightly (~+15ms) but tail improved ~30%; throughput dropped ~7%.
3) Pin to dedicated kernel build (v5.19-rt) vs stock (v6.2) on a dev host:
   - Result: dev host with older kernel still had spikes; kernel difference unlikely primary cause.
4) Run sampler on a host with CPU isolation (cset shield) to reduce co-scheduled containers:
   - Result: spike incidence reduced by ~45% (points to noisy neighbors / scheduler preemption).

Hypotheses (ranked):
A) Short-lived CPU preemption from background housekeeping (container-level cron jobs, vm-swappiness events) causes scheduling jitter that amplifies tail when batch sizes are small. Evidence: run-queue surges and improvement with CPU isolation.
B) KV-cache eviction + on-demand cache rebuild path causes intermittent long token processing when cache-miss paths run synchronized maintenance. Evidence: eviction_rate correlated with some spikes, and disabling kv-cache reduced incidence.
C) Batching heuristic front-of-queue fragmentation: when many small requests interleave, the effective batch size shrinks causing more frequent kernel invocations and overhead. Evidence: observed mean_batch drop at spike times and improvement when increasing delay_ms.
D) Rare kernel/syscall stall triggered by a specific I/O path (less likely): trace shows no I/O bottleneck, and kernel swap tests were negative.

Short-term mitigations recommended (can be applied during business hours):
- Temporarily increase per-host batching delay to 20–30ms for interactive profile (owner: Ethan) — reduces tail at cost of marginal latency increase.
- Add low-overhead cpu shielding for inference processes on at-risk hosts (owner: SRE oncall) — schedule: nightly roll, monitor for regressions.
- Rollout a KV-cache backoff experiment: on heavy eviction, enter degraded-mode where we temporarily switch to smaller cache size with async rebuild (owner: Luis).

Runbook for on-call bench engineers (quick steps):
1) If spikes detected, run the isolated tail sampler command (see above) targeting 1 host. Confirm reproducibility within 20m.
2) Collect perf counters: top -H -p <serving-pid>, /proc/schedstat, iostat -xz 1 30, nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv -l 1 --duration=30
3) Trigger a 90s eBPF off-cpu trace (rbpf) and save the flame SVG to artifacts.
4) If run-queue >6 and sched_switch spikes visible, escalate to SRE to check host-level cronjobs/cgroup throttling.
5) As temporary fix, change delay_ms and observe p95 for 10m; revert if user-visible regressions worsen.

Open action items (owners and ETA):
- Ethan: create a canary change to interactive profile with delay_ms=25 and run A/B for 24h (ETA: 2026-03-22).
- Luis: prototype KV-cache soft-degrade mode (async rebuild) and bench locally (ETA: 2026-03-24).
- Hannah: add automated tracer collection to the sampler test harness and wire artifact upload to the perf S3 path (ETA: 2026-03-26).
- Priya: update JIRA-PI-3742 with collected artifacts and upload flame/svg + traces (ETA: 2026-03-20 end of day).

Decisions made in this sync:
- Do not change kernel or perform host reboots during peak daytime hours.
- Prioritize software mitigations (batching, cache behavior) before large infra changes.

Notes / Follow-ups for retrospective:
- Add a lightweight host health telemetry that captures short-window run-queue and scheduler preemption counts; current telemetry granularity masks sub-second bursts.
- Revisit batching heuristic: consider adaptive delay that increases briefly when batch sizes drop below a threshold.
- Run a controlled noisy-neighbor test (spin CPU on co-located container) to quantify sensitivity.
